name: Camilism
summary: Camilism is the revolutionary Christian thought of the Colombian priest and sociologist Camilo Torres Restrepo, built on 'effective love': love of neighbour must be made effective, which requires taking power from the privileged minority for the poor majority, by peaceful means if they do not resist and by force if they do. His 1965 United Front programme joins land reform without compensation, State ownership of banks, resources and health care, compulsory planning and progressive taxation with political pluralism, cooperation with communists on common goals and a refusal to join the Communist Party.
scope: Torres's own political writings and speeches of 1962-1966, above all the 1965 United Front platforms (the Medellin and Bogota versions), his Messages in the Frente Unido newspaper, the 1963 lecture on democracy, and the 1965 essay on the Christian imperative to revolution, read with Herrera Farfan's scholarly study of effective love. It does not cover later guerrilla conduct of the ELN, other liberation theologies or Marxism-Leninism generally, and no regime applied it, so there is no record beyond Torres's own words. His 1966 turn to the armed road was brief, so his peaceful-or-forced stance of 1965 counts as the mature one.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The platform commits the State to a comprehensive social-security plan that guarantees health and medical care free to the population.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The sources record no position on this, and no stated principle bears on it.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Torres argued that without the State directing investment by compulsory plan no efficiency in favour of the majority is possible, and the programme abolishes free enterprise.

public-ownership.rationale: The platform places banks, insurance, hospitals, public transport, radio and television and natural resources in State hands, with oil exploited by the State.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The tax plank charges a progressive tax on income above a decorous family level and passes any surplus not invested under the plan to the State.

unions-good.rationale: He treats unions and strikes as building revolutionary consciousness and wants workers organised in unions to share in running firms, while condemning government-bought leaders.

property-fundamental.rationale: The platform expropriates land without compensation where the common good requires it and gives title to those who work it, so private property is not an overriding right.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Every public or private investment must fit the compulsory national plan, and foreign oil concessions are tied to State share, refining and wage conditions.

cut-welfare.rationale: The programme builds an integral and progressive social-security scheme covering unemployment, disability, old age and death.

worker-ownership.rationale: The Medellin programme replaces free enterprise with cooperative and community enterprise and lets workers hold shares and take part in direction and profits.

missingStatements.text: Opposition movements should boycott elections that a ruling elite controls.
missingStatements.rationale: Torres practised and argued active abstention in 1965 because the electoral machinery is controlled by the oligarchy and opposition in parliament only lends it a democratic cover.

quotes.text: Personalmente yo soy partidario de la abstención electoral pero no de una abstención pasiva, sino de una abstención activa, beligerante y revolucionaria.
quotes.where: Camilo Torres, archivochile text ct0029 (see source s6)

quotes.text: La abstención electoral, por sí sola, no es un arma de combate revolucionaria; ella tiene que estar acompañada de una organización y de una disciplina beligerante y activa.

quotes.text: nosotros no podemos ir a hacerle el juego a las oligarquías metiéndonos en su sistema electoral, controlado por ellas

notes: Searched every theme in Torres's collected 1960-66 texts on archivochile (platforms, messages, interviews, lectures) and Marxists Internet Archive messages, and keyword-searched the 1985 Escritos volume (not cited). Government, economy and world themes are well covered by the platforms; liberty, culture, ecology, technology and most society themes are unaddressed and stay null (no mention of drugs, guns, abortion, same-sex marriage, climate or nuclear power was found). The platform's two versions differ (Medellin allows cooperative or State transport and sets oil conditions at 80 percent and 10 years; the later Bogota text 70 percent and 25 years); answers rest on points they share. Wikipedia's definition of Camilism as including later Montoneros or Sandinista currents was not used.
